subtopic: PROPOSED NATION-WIDE TOUR BY HOUSE COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: PROPOSED NATION-WIDE TOUR BY HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago I announced plans for a coast to coast tour by the house committee on agriculture. We have worked out a tentative itinerary which will take the committee into every province over a two week period. We had hoped to be able to organize this tour for early August, but I wish to inform the house now that this has not been possible, for several reasons. In the first place, we have been unable to charter a suitable aircraft during August for the two week period we estimate the tour will take. Another obstacle to having the tour during August is the problem of booking accommodation for such a large group at the height of the tourist season. We also thought committee members might find the weather rather unpleasantly hot for the kind of intensive itinerary, including long bus rides through the countryside, at this time of year. For all these reasons we have decided to postpone the tour for a few weeks.
A suitable aircraft is available for late September and early October, and we now expect to take the committee on this tour of the country at that time to see our farm problems as they really are, the better, we hope, to deal with them in parliament in the future.

subtopic: COST OF PENSIONS AT 65 AND 70
COST OF PENSIONS AT 65 AND 70
speechtext:
1.	According to government actuaries, how many persons in Canada will have reached 65 years of age by January 1. 1965?
2.	How many will have reached 70 years of age?
3.	What amount would the government have to pay, on that same date, in order to give everyone a pension of $100 a month (a) at age 65 (b) at age 70?
4.	What amount would the government have to pay, starting on January 1, 1965, in order to give everyone a pension of $150 a month (a) at age 65 (b) at age 70?
5.	By what percentage would income tax and corporation taxes have to be increased in order to cover these expenditures each year?
6.	What amount of income tax would a person earning $5,000 a year, married and with two children have to pay in order to cover expenditures under parts 3 and 4 above?

Answer: 1, 2, 3 and 4. Based on a set of projections of the 1961 census population developed last year in connection with actuarial studies on the Canada pension plan, as described in the actuarial report dated August 30, 1963, and tabled in parliament on October 15, 1963, the chief actuary of the department of insurance has estimated that on January 1, 1965, there would be in Canada 1,469,000 persons aged 65 or over and 960,000 persons aged 70 or over. He has also estimated that, for the calendar year 1965, it would cost $1,822 million to pay $100 per month to persons aged 65 or over in that year, $1,190 million to pay $100 per month to persons aged 70 or over, $2,733 million to pay $150 per month to persons aged 65 or over and $1,785 million to pay $150 per month to persons aged 70 or over. These costs, based on the aforementioned set of population projections, were adjusted to take account of past and anticipated future experience under the old age security program.
5.	In order to raise an amount of revenue equal to the amount by which the above estimated costs exceed the expenditures forecast for the present old age security pensions the budgetary revenue from income tax on individuals and corporations combined would have to be increased by approximately the following percentages:
For pensions of $100 per month payable at age 65, 27 per cent; for pensions of $100 per month payable at age 70, 9 per cent; for pensions of $150 per month payable at age 65, 53 per cent; for pensions of $150 per month payable at age 70, 26 per cent.
Increases of this magnitude in present rates of tax would in some cases be impractical. For example, if the present top rate of personal income tax, which is 80 per cent before provincial abatement, were increased by 27 per cent it would become 101.6 per cent. If the present corporation income tax rate of 47 per cent before provincial abatement were

Questions
increased by 27 per cent it would become 59.7 per cent and if increased by 53 per cent it would become 71.9 per cent.
6.	If the personal income tax payable by a married taxpayer with income of $5,000, who had two dependant children qualified for family allowance (which is $237.79 at current rates after deducting a provincial abatement at 21 per cent) were increased by the percentages shown above the additional amounts of tax payable would be as follows:
Increases of 27 per cent, $64; increase of 9 per cent, $21; increase of 53 per cent, $126; increase of 26 per cent, $62.
However, because it would be impractical to increase the tax of all individuals by 53 per cent or even by 27 per cent, the amount of tax paid by individuals with lower or medium incomes would have to be increased by more than the percentages shown above in order to produce the revenue proposed. As a result the taxpayer described in this question would have to pay larger amounts of additional tax than shown above. An increase of 27 per cent or even 9 per cent would have a very appreciable effect on the tax of all individuals.

subtopic: STUDY OF INFLATION
speechtext:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CRASH OF T.C.A. PLANE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CRASH OF T.C.A. PLANE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport; I wish to assure him it has nothing to do with the Jet Star. I wonder if he could tell me if the inquiry into the DC-8 crash at Ste. Therese has now been completed and when we can expect the findings to be made public.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CRASH OF T.C.A. PLANE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has asked a question about a very grave matter about which there is a great deal of concern. He was good enough to give me notice in ample time for me to prepare a reply. I do not usually read a reply, but in view of the gravity of the circumstances and their tragic nature I would not wish to use any words which had not been carefully considered. Perhaps the house would permit me to read the answer instead of speaking extemporaneously.
The transport department's investigation of the T.C.A. DC-8 crash at Ste. Thdrese, Quebec last November is expected to be completed by mid-September. The investigators have recovered 105,000 pounds or 76 per cent of the aircraft structure, all of which has been minutely examined by technical specialists. Significant items have also been studied and dissected in laboratories together with scrap sized pieces of metal which it would be impracticable to retrieve but from which samples have been taken. An estimated 90 per cent of the structure can now be accounted for.
The investigation, which I am told is the largest in Canadian aviation history, has been carried out by six working groups under the general direction of the chief of accident investigation division of the Department of Transport. Each group is headed by a government employee either of the Department of Transport, the national research council or the R.C.A.F., and consists of experts drawn from the government, T.C.A., United Aircraft Corporation, Canadair and the Canadian air line pilots association. The investigation team is concerned only with the determination of facts, and it is not their responsibility to allocate blame.
At the moment reports from the laboratories and specialists are being analysed. When this is completed the findings will come to me as Minister of Transport. I will have the responsibility to decide whether a

Inquiries of the Ministry board of inquiry is to be convened at which the findings of the investigators would be presented at a public hearing. If such a board is convened it will consist of persons who are not employed in the Department of Transport or T.C.A.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-110, to facilitate the making of loans to students.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the short time I spoke last night, I pointed out that federal-provincial relations today have reached a climax, since they tend more and more towards the establishment of a Unitarian system rather than a federal one. So much so that the bill now before us constitutes a federal government intrusion in a field which, under section 93 of the British North America Act, is assigned exclusively to the provinces.
I also reminded the house that several judgments of the privy council had established that provinces could not do indirectly what they were not allowed to do directly. One can find in Hansard certain cases related to the study of this matter of constitutional jurisdiction.
I pointed out also that the co-operative federalism advocated by our hon. friends opposite is a disguised, hypocritical, camouflaged and diplomatic method of centralization, such as we knew it under the governments of prime ministers King and St. Laurent.
Loans to Students
I pointed out that the bill under consideration is an interference of the federal government in the field of education.
Allow me to refer to a speech made before the house in 1958 by Hon. Donald Fleming, the then minister of finance, at a time when the matter of grants to universities was discussed. As reported at page 4726 of Hansard, he stated:
We recognize and we respect the provinces' absolute jurisdiction in the field of education. The increased grants proposed by the government are merely a necessary aid to universities, without government infringement upon a single provincial responsibility. As long as this government is in power, it will never encroach upon education, which is a provincial matter.
My argument is based on this statement of the former minister of finance.
It is also based on a very important statement made by the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) in March last, in Toronto. Here is what the parliamentary secretary of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce said, according to the report of the newspaper La Presse of Thursday, March 19, 1964, which I quote:
As soon as they were announced, the federal loans to students were condemned by the provincial government and the Quebec students themselves. That was to be expected, for which autonomist can interpret such distribution of funds for education purposes otherwise than as a flagrant interference in a provincial field?
Up to this week, however, no Liberal member, as far as we know, had publicly objected to such action.
It was Mr. Jean-Luc Pepin, Drummond-Artha-baska, assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who took action in this respect in Toronto on Monday night.
And I quote:
"The provinces, he said, would discharge this responsibility more efficiently." Yet, Ottawa might, he thinks, facilitate the development of universities by resorting to loans from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and continue to distribute postgraduate fellowships through the Canada council and the national research council. But when it comes to loans and scholarships to students in general, that is a "real provocation".
I wonder whether the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska will repeat the same ideas and argue in the same way when we discuss this legislation. I understand that the hon. member may have had some serious reasons for being absent yesterday, but we find that today he is still absent.
The author of the article, Mr. Larochelle, says further:
Mr. Pepin considers all this as many others do (the English language dailies, for instance, among which the Montreal Gazette of February 24, 1964),

Loans to Students
but to proclaim it and sound the alarm as a government member, that is quite another thing.
And Mr. Larochelle adds:
Well done, Mr. Pepin. You might give some of your courage to your colleagues on the treasury benches.
The door is now open to you members from Quebec, who, like myself, come from the most autonomist province.
I do not see many who have the courage to denounce that centralizing legislation which this government has introduced. Anyway, Mr. Speaker, nobody need be shocked if I attack a measure which I consider to be anticonstitutional, since the students themselves, through the students' association of Quebec, recently expressed their views most vigorously and, in spite of their needs, in spite of the aid which student loans would represent, had the courage to sacrifice this mess of pot-age offered to them, because it was an intrusion into the field which the province of Quebec considers most sacred, that is the educational field.
Indeed-and this is a strange coincidence -a well known columnist, Mr. Paul Sauriol, just wrote in Le Devoir, which is generally quite sympathetic to our friends opposite, an editorial published today about the problem of student loans and co-operative federalism.
It is unfortunate that the Quebec leader, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), should be referred to in this article, because these are not necessarily his views, especially on this matter of federal intrusion into the field of civil rights, as I intend to point out to him shortly. Mr. Sauriol, referring to the recent break between the two Quebec Liberal organizations in the federal and provincial fields, quoted a statement made by the Minister of Justice at the convention held recently in Quebec city:
In a sound provincial system, both levels of government fully respect the jurisdiction and responsibilities of either one.
What a wonderful theory. What a poor showing.
That is a clear and unqualified text on the requirements of federalism. In the Canadian constitution, education comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces: however, Mr. Favreau, as a minister in the Pearson government, proposes and commends those federal loans to students, which are an invasion of provincial jurisdiction.
Today, prominent jurists of the province of Quebec who sit on the other side-I can see my hon. friend from Argenteuil-Deux-Mon-tagnes (Mr. Drouin) and the member for St.

Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner)-will analyse very carefully, I hope, the point concerning the constitutionality of this bill.
I proceed with Mr. Sauriol's article:
That is a clear and unqualified text on the requirements of federalism. But, in the Canadian constitution, education comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces; however, Mr. Favreau, as minister in the Pearson government, proposes and commends those federal loans to students, which are an invasion of provincial jurisdiction. According to Mr. Favreau's own definition, it can be said that the confederation is sick.
-That is what is called respecting the rights of the provinces.
The journalist comments upon a statement made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), and Mr. Sauriol continues:
That system remains unacceptable because the central government is taking the initiative in matters which fall exclusively under provincial jurisdiction, collecting and using taxes in that way for provincial purposes, imposing controls and the terms of its program even to the provinces which would like to be kept out of it.
I know that my friends opposite will refer to that provision of the bill, in section 12 and the following clauses, which concerns alternative payments, but I do not believe that some of my friends opposite will favour such an evident breach of the Canadian constitution. I have a right to wonder, as they should themselves, why there is in Quebec a nationalism crisis?
We do not have to look further than the disrespect of the British North America Act. If the federal government had respected the text and the spirit of the confederation, the province of Quebec would not be facing that surge of nationalism which becomes necessary, under certain circumstances, to hold in check the centralizing efforts of bureaucrats who exercised their evil and autocratic influence in 1951, under the St. Laurent and King administrations. Some of them are now sitting on cabinet benches and they have only one objective, push down the throat of the nation a unitary system, at the expense of federalism which is so necessary to the development of the rights, the prerogatives and the very existence of the province of Quebec.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Ask Mr. Diefenbaker.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member wishes to ask a question, I suggest he should rise and do so.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, could the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere tell us whether he is giving his personal

opinion, that of his party or that of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker)?

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am giving my personal opinion, and for the information of the hon. member for Beauhamois-Salaberry, I must say that as a member from the province of Quebec, it is my sacred responsibility to defend the education system which was the very source of our progress, of our development in the province of Quebec, and my hon. friend has no right to be a traitor to the con-federative act.
The hon. member may very well preach in favour of compulsory military enrolment, but that will not bring salvation to the province of Quebec which intends to go on living and developing under our system of confederation, provided, as I said earlier, that the spirit as well as the letter of the confederation pact is adhered to.	.
Mr. Speaker, as I said a moment ago, Bill No. C-110 constitutes a glaring intrusion by the federal government into an exclusively provincial field. Moreover, it constitutes an encroachment upon the most elementary principle of Quebec's civil code. I again ask the great legal minds sitting on the government side to assist me in considering section 15 of the bill before us, which reads as follows:
A guaranteed student loan made by a bank to a borrower not of full age, and interest thereon other than interest payable under section 6, is recoverable by a bank from the borrower as though the borrower had been of full age at the time the loan was made.
Shame, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hear the hon. member for Longueuil say: Oh, oh. It would have been better for him to spend a few months at the university in order to acquire a few legal notions, for he would have known that civil law comes exclusively under the provinces, that the question of majority is a civil law matter into which the federal government has no right to intervene, as it is now doing.
I would suggest that the hon. member for Longueuil ask his colleagues, the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Drouin), the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner), the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) whether the question of majority comes under the civil code of the province of Quebec, especially sections 242 and following.
Loans to Students
This piece of federal legislation clearly goes against the provisions of the civil code. I am not familiar with the civil law of the other provinces, but I am speaking here as a Quebec member. What will happen when a minor is taken to court under this bill? The only way to get out of the lawsuit will be to have it thrown out of court on a technicality as provided in the code of civil procedure of the province of Quebec.
At that time, what should be the decision of the court? What legal obligation will this legislation impose on the counsel? The latter will have first of all to plead the unconstitutionality of this legislation, since civil law is the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. And I challenge anybody among the members opposite to contradict the fact that the question of majority is one of civil right exclusively reserved to the provinces, as clearly and specifically established by section 242 and the following sections in the civil code of the province of Quebec, and accordingly, in the rules of procedure that may be found in section 164 and following of the code of civil procedure of the province of Quebec?
Mr. Speaker, other questions are also at stake. Let us therefore read the other sections of this bill. Let us see what is said in paragraph (a) of section 13:
The governor In council may make regulations (a) prescribing the forms of agreements-
The federal government will now interfere in a civil action taken by a citizen of another province. Another intrusion of the federal government in the field of civil liability. The governor in council will interfere to amend the provisions of the civil code concerning the amendment of an agreement between a borrower, on one hand, and a bank, on the other.
You might state that, in that instance, there is a federal legal provision, since the federal Bank Act is involved. I admit this point, but, then, we are concerned with an action of mixed character, from a legal point of view, an action of joint jurisdiction. What steps will the minister take concerning the wording of the bill, which once again, infringes on the civil code of the province of Quebec?
Paragraph d) of clause 13 reads as follows:
The governor in council may make regulations providing for the assignment or transfer-
This is another measure of civil law which can be found in section 1155 and the following sections of the code of civil law of the province of Quebec, while the question of subrogation is a matter of civil law in which

Loans to Students
the federal government cannot interfere. It is another interference of the federal government in a field of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
There are other measures which affect civil law, property rights. And now the federal government interferes in another provincial field, by virtue of provisions of paragraph (k), section 13, which reads as follows:
The governor in council may make regulations prescribing the maximum number of academic years-
Here is another direct and baneful interference of the federal government, which is to decide on the number of years during which a citizen of a province-and I speak of the province of Quebec-will have to go to school or college in order to be granted a certificate or a diploma. This is the exclusive jurisdiction of the minister of education in the province of Quebec and the federal government has no right to interfere in that field. I would like to hear some adverse comments from the legal minds.
Another matter, Mr. Speaker. Paragraph (n) of section 13 provides that:
The governor in council may make regulations prescribing the method of determining when the student is or ceases to be a full time student.
If this is not complete interference of the federal government in the field of education -and I am speaking of the province of Quebec-what is it?
This legislation is further proof of the fact that we have another centralizing government in office but that was a characteristic attitude of all the Liberal administrations we have had in Canada since the second world war and especially since 1939.
That is not all. Paragraph (p) of section 13 provides:
The governor in council may make regulations prescribing any other matter or thing that under this act is to be prescribed or prescribed by the regulations.
That leaves the door wide open for the worst abuses and intrusions on the part of the federal government concerning the regulations adopted by the various provincial departments of education.
I see my hon. friend, the member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) shaking his head in denial. But let him stand up and ask a legal question. We are not going to turn this into a political problem, because unfortunately we have too often been slaves to a political party. That is why today we must set aside partisanship when the respect of the Canadian constitution is at stake, a constitution

which allows for the development and overlapping of two cultures, two races, two languages willing to work for the greatness and prosperity of Canada as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, there are other means of helping students. The provinces have also imperious needs in view of their present development, which is really going at a dizzy speed in Quebec, and I am proud to point it out.
But will this measure solve the educational problem in the province of Quebec? With all respect, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that it will not, and I say that the federal government should, while complying with the constitution, make more generous concessions to the provinces, under the form of unconditional equalization payments. Provincial authorities could then enact legislation concerning education and pass measures which would meet the true regional needs of the various categories of students in the province of Quebec.
According to our hon. friends, there would be an escape clause in this bill. I admit that the option formula could be of some use in the present circumstances. I appreciate the fact that clause 12 of the bill provides for alternative payments, but it is precisely to this principle that I, as many others, am opposed. There is, of course, this way out which makes it possible to vote in favour of this bill, because it provides for alternative payments to the provinces.
But time has come to put a stop to the federal intrusion in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
In 1958-59, under the Conservative administration, we solved a disputable question, the one concerning university grants. Yesterday, the Leader of the Opposition pointed out the outstanding work accomplished to that effect by the late premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Paul Sauve.
But we have not solved this problem; we have solved it only on a temporary basis, in spite of one concession which I would not call pernicious, but generous; indeed, as I said a while ago and as is specifically defined in the British North America Act, education is under the exclusive control of the provinces, the federal government's interference being justified only in cases where the minority rights would be at stake.
It is a pity that the federal government, of whatever political colour, did not act more often to enforce the rights of the minorities in provinces other than the province of Quebec, so that these minorities would get

lair treatment similar to that given the English minority in the province of Quebec. The federal government's intervention would have been justified in such a case, and it might have prevented this nationalism crisis which affects the whole of Canada today. This would have been the only possible condition for the federal government intervening in the education field, and not the introduction of this legislation which is bringing up again the matter of the minorities' privileges and rights.
No, Mr. Speaker. Since the last war we have been witnessing a continual intrusion in the provincial fields on the part of the federal government. On a pretext of war urgency, provinces have been asked to yield their rights. They agreed to do so because those rights were to be returned to them as soon as the war would be over, but since then, the federal government has refused to reconvey those rights to the provinces.
That is why we are forced to consider all sorts of compromise, liable to sharpen the nationalistic requirements of those who have had enough of being dealt with unfairly by the federal government, whatever party is in office.
Mr. Speaker, the principle of responsibilitysharing is not admissible and unfortunately, I cannot support the argument that a department of education should be established in Ottawa at the present time. I am against this principle because education comes within the provincial jurisdiction. I am not any more in favour of setting up a committee on education. The present government has enough responsibilities as it is. It must solve the unemployment problem, that of the constant rise of the cost of living, the various economic problems, not to mention eastern agriculture.
Why should they now want to legislate in a field which does not concern them?
I would say to my Liberal friends, look after your own problems. You have plenty. And if you really want to promote education in Canada, be more generous to the provinces, so they can carry out the education programs they have laid out.
I respect and share the opinion of my English speaking colleagues who, in the circumstances, can easily vote for this bill, because the nine other provinces do not have the education system ours has. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, those nine other provinces have the same culture, the same language, the same religion, while the language, culture and history of the province of Quebec are different.

We speak of respect for the constitution. When the fathers of confederation accepted the constitution in 1867, it was because they saw in it an opportunity to survive. Prior to that, there had been a separate system, which had not given good results and had not settled the problem of the two great races then facing one another. The Union Act was followed by the British North America Act, which the people of Quebec generously supported because they thought-as they still do-that it was their last hope. Indeed, the British North America Act does contain legislative provisions for the respect of the rights of minorities, of whatever race they may be.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I will vote against that bill. It does not matter if I am the only one of my party to do so. I respect the ideas of my Conservative colleagues and I understand that they may vote in favour of that legislation, on account of the provisions for substitution payments. But basically this legislation is an intrusion into the educational field, and as long as this government does not respect education and educational freedom in the province of Quebec, I will consider it my duty to object to any legislation which it will introduce.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after having heard the firm speech of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) who is an eminent expert in constitutional law, I find it extremely difficult to speak in favour of the bill concerning student loans.
However, I will try to bring to the debate the contribution of the head of a family whose three children are attending university. I met him yesterday morning and asked him what he thought of the joint statement made by university student groups. He replied: "Those children are unaware of the problems of the head of a family who is racking his brains to pay the university studies of his children."
Then, of course, a father does not see the problem in the same light as an expert in constitutional law. The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) is, however, fully justified when he insists on the rights of Quebec in that field, and I heartily approve him.
I also know, however, that certain pedagogues disagree somewhat on educational matters with experts in constitutional law.
For instance, I remember reading not so long ago a speech delivered by Mr. Treffie Boulanger, of Montreal, one of the most

Loans to Students
prominent pedagogues of the province of Quebec, where he advocated the establishment of a federal department of education, precisely for the following reason: "Because, he said, there are over 1.5 million French Canadians in other provinces, and such a department would help them to preserve their language." This is one of the major problems in Canada and it might be one of the basic reasons put forward by those who advocate the secession of Quebec, because they see that their fellow citizens in the other provinces are losing what they are the most attached to, namely their language and often their faith.
But today, as a member of the federal parliament, I must also think, without forgetting my Quebec fellow citizens, about that million and a half of my compatriots whom I visited on some occasions in the various provinces of Canada, and whom I want to support and assist.
I know that this legislation will certainly help them to become Canadians on an equal footing with our English speaking compatriots. I feel that those compatriots have the right to go to the university and to improve their minds, and this legislation will certainly benefit them. That is why if, in theory, I have reasons to be against that kind of violation of the constitutional rights of Quebec, all the same in practice I am in favour of this legislation which will enable thousands of my compatriots in other provinces-and I mean French speaking and English speaking Canadians-to continue their studies at the university.
About that matter, in particular, I would like to read to the house a statement made by Hon. Mr. Lesage. According to the Quebec city newspaper L'Evenement, he said to the Prime Minister of Canada and the provincial premiers:
-the only way to solve the problem was for the federal government to give hack to Quebec fiscal compensation which will equal the amounts spent to reimburse the interest on student loans made by banks and other institutions, taking into account the relative proportion of the Quebec population.
In my opinion, the letter and the spirit of the legislation seem to be consistent with that statement at the present time.
Now, I should like to deal with a point which was raised yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and stressed by other speakers who preceded me, but I want nevertheless to refer thereto, because it is a statement that surprised me enormously,

coming from a financial expert. I heard the Minister of Finance say that banks lend only the money of their depositors.
I think that he made a slip, because certainly he would not have made such a statement. In my opinion, he is a very responsible man who is quite familiar with the chartered banks act. At all events, may I quote from page 1088 of the Canada Year Book for 1962, which says:
-the central bank can determine within broad limits the total amount of chartered banks assets and deposits-
This is the important point.
-but leaves the allocation of bank credit and other forms of credit to the private sector of the economy.
What does that mean? It means that any allocation of credit in Canada is made through chartered banks. On the other hand, I might also quote, for instance, one of the great economists that several members of the house certainly know, namely Mr. Paul Samuelson who, in his book entitled "Economics", says on page 204:
Credit establishments or commercial banks are the only organizations able to supply bank money or script money that can conveniently be used as payment instruments. Such is their main role and function.
And on 221, the same great economist, Mr. Samuelson, goes on to say:
The bankers say: We can only invest the money that our clients leave with us. We create nothing. We only put to work the savings of the community.
Mr. Samuelson declares that the bankers who support this argument are completely in error.
I think that Mr. Samuelson uses the words "are completely in error" because he is very polite, for there are other words to say that.
Perhaps, I could quote a hundred other utterances to prove to the Minister of Finance that bank credit is really created by the chartered banks, and that they do not simply loan their clients' savings. I could also quote economists, bankers, professors, financial analysts from various countries of the world to support this argument.
Of course, it is unthinkable that such a statement should have been made by the minister, but, as I have said a while ago, it is surely a slip of the tongue.
I noticed that in his opening remarks the minister congratulated certain organizations which have already granted loans to students throughout Canada. Here I want to point out that he may not be aware of what we succeeded in doing in the province of Quebec.

I would like to mention before all hon. members the wonderful work done by the St. Jean Baptiste society of Quebec which created, almost 15 years ago, what is called the student loan of honour. Several million dollars have already been loaned to students by that organization in the last 15 years. It all started in Montreal and then spread throughout the province of Quebec. I, myself, was the founder and administrator of one of those student loan funds, and I am very glad to take this opportunity to commend the St. Jean Baptiste society of the province of Quebec for their wonderful work in that field, which permitted thousands of students to continue their university studies.
Neither should we forget the work done by the Artisans society which also created special loan funds for students, and those loans of honour are without interest. That is much better than what we proposed to do under this bill. Loans without any interest at all. Students repay only the amounts loaned on their honour and, up to now, results have been wonderful, since there have been practically no losses.
I should also like to take this opportunity to mention the work done by the l'Assomp-tion society in Moncton, New Brunswick, which, through the modest contribution received, made it possible to educate, in Acadia, a whole elite perhaps which was able to take advantage of scholarships given to students in this area of our country.
Another thing I note here is that obviously, in this bill, the minister, just as in the case of several other bills, will once more take money out of the national treasury or the consolidated revenue fund. It is wonderful, I think, to have this inexhaustible source where we can always get capital. It seems that it is always there. However, the taxpayers should not forget that they are the ones who are constantly called upon to replenish the federal treasury, because it is fed through the most odious means possible, that is tax increases.
There are other solutions and we have advocated them in this house on many occasions. The Minister of Finance, who is an extremely intelligent man, is familiar with those proposals, because the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson)) has asked him questions which have remained unanswered until now. For instance, he pointed out that certain financing operations are carried out through the Bank of Canada at present. Since 20220-350

that seems quite certain, I wish to congratulate the minister for having taken the initiative of allowing the Bank of Canada to finance certain government expenditures or outlays.
I should like to quote also a prominent economist, Mr. Samuelson, who said that certain American economists are asking for what we, in this group have been advocating for 30 or 40 years, as can be seen on page 211 of his book entitled "Economics":
A substantial group of American economists are advocating nowadays a radical reform of the banking system which would bring back a system of 100 per cent liquid cover on all deposits at call. That would be the only honest system in which banks would not be creating new money for their profitable purposes, usurping at the same time the royal prerogatives reserved to the government under the constitution. Finally, that would be the only neutral system, in that the banks would not create money during boom periods, thus adding fuel to the fire of inflation and would not reduce the offer of money during panic or depression periods, thus increasing deflation, bankruptcies and unemployment.
I know that since we gave so many explanations, several hon. members sitting on the government side are in favour of taking over of the royal prerogatives by the federal government, and that is becoming increasingly necessary and urgent. I think that before long the government will recover the royal prerogatives which should never have been conceded in any way to chartered banks.
Mr. Speaker, those are the few observations I had to make on this bill which I think will relieve many family heads who are faced with the nightmare that is for them the financing of their son's education.
Now, this new legislation will enable our children to achieve a higher education.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my good friend the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote) opened his remarks by saying that he was going to speak from the practical knowledge of a good friend of his who was the father of three students within the age group that might benefit by this legislation, and he contrasted himself in this respect with the hon. member for Ber-thier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) because he said that this hon. member had spoken as an expert on constitutional law. I am torn between the two roles, Mr. Speaker. I have three children of the age of university students, who may be in serious need; I do not know. The regulations have not been published yet, so I am not sure how needy you

Loans to Students
have to be. I do not intend to speak on that point of view, however practical it may be, but rather as one who has had some experience of constitutional law and is much concerned by what I believe to be very grave defects that may destroy the effectiveness of this particular legislation.
I do not propose to repeat the qualified approval of this bill that was expressed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Webster). I agree with what they said, and I adopt what the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway said, that the bill merits support on the theory that half a loaf is better than no bread. But as I have said, I fear that the effectiveness of this bill is seriously jeopardized by certain technical and constitutional defects. The matter has already been referred to in the house by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). Since they referred to this matter I have had the opportunity to give consideration to the constitutional problem involved in the bill as it is at present drafted, and I would like to give a warning to the government and to this house that I think there is a very great doubt whether the bill as at present drafted may not totally fail because of technical and constitutional defects.
I am not dealing with the argument that has been presented, that because the bill deals with education, the provisions of section 93 of the British North America Act bring its subject matter within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. On that matter I may say that I found the arguments of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) quite convincing and I do not propose to add to them or to discuss the matter further. But the real difficulty lies in the fact that the key provisions of this bill delegate to the lieutenant governors in council of the various provinces, under clause 2(b) and (k), the duty to designate appropriate authorities to issue certificates of eligibility for loans under the act and also to designate institutions of learning that are qualified to give courses in respect of which loans are to be made available.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the key questions of what students are qualified by need and by satisfactory scholastic standing and what institutions of learning fall within the purview of the legislation are to be determined, not by this legislation itself but by

such persons as are authorized by the provincial cabinets, the lieutenant governors in council.
Let me make it abundantly clear that I am not objecting to the substance of this division of responsibility. What I question is the legal power of this parliament to delegate such power to the lieutenant governors in council in the absence of provincial legislation vesting that power in the lieutenant governors in council. I will spare the house a lecture on the constitutional and legal questions involved. I have been counsel in some of the leading cases on this subject and I have a nodding acquaintance with the technical problems involved. It will perhaps suffice, in order that this matter may be fully looked into, to say that the Supreme Court of Canada decided in the Nova Scotia interdelegation case in 1951- anyone interested can find it in the 1951 Supreme Court Reports-that interdelegation between the dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures was unconstitutional. I agree that this case is not the same as the present case, in that here we have, not an attempt to delegate from the parliament of Canada to the legislatures of the provinces, but an attempt to delegate from the parliament of Canada to the provincial executives. But I think the same principle is applicable to both cases.
It is a well recognized fact that parliament can delegate powers to a subordinate agency, but the lieutenant governor in council is in no sense a subordinate agency of this parliament. His duties are defined by the British North America Act itself. I see the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Pennell) making notes. He might be interested to know, that the duties of the lieutenant governor in council are defined in section 65 of the British North America Act. It would, as I say, be possible to delegate to a subordinate agency, but by no argument can the lieutenant governor in council, under the powers granted to him by the British North America Act which are quite independent of the powers of parliament, be considered a subordinate agency.
Another thing that I recognize as possible is for the parliament of Canada to delegate authority to a provincial board or body upon which power has been conferred by provincial statute. Once again I refer my hon. friend, who I think is particularly interested, to the Prince Edward Island potato reference case found in 1952 Supreme Court Reports, where it was made clear that this parliament had the right to give to a marketing board set up

and authorized to receive powers by provincial legislation the power to administer federal legislation. That power is all right, but so far as I know no provincial statute is in existence authorizing the lieutenant governors in council to receive or exercise the powers and duties imposed upon them by the legislation we are now considering.
I have no doubt that the governments of the provinces would be very happy to invite the legislatures of their respective provinces, if they are going to avail themselves of this scheme, to pass the necessary enabling legislation, but that hardly seems practicable at the present time. I have no doubt that the minister and the house are anxious that clear and full authority should be given so that this scheme can go into effect in the next scholastic year. I do not suppose that the legislatures of the provinces are going to be in session before that time. Therefore they will not be able to confer this power, and without it I repeat that there is very grave doubt whether this parliament can impose a duty upon the lieutenant governors in council which has not been imposed by the legislatures of the provinces themselves.
I suggest that a solution might be to amend the present provisions of the bill and confer the power to designate authorized institutions of learning on the governor in council, upon nomination or recommendation of the lieutenant governors in council. In that case the actual appointment would be made by an agency subordinate to this parliament. I do not speak disrespectfully of the governor general in council when I say that agency is subordinate to this parliament. That I think is well recognized. While the actual appointment would be made by them the real choice, the decision, would be made by the provincial authorities, and the rights of the provinces with regard to education would be preserved and recognized in this way.
I hope the government will give serious consideration to the suggestion I have made. Personally I do not believe that the unsupported statement that the Department of Justice thinks it is all right is good enough authority for this house. This is not the occasion for me to express my views about the Department of Justice. I will have occasion to do that, I hope, before too long and my views may not be too kindly. However that may be, I say that this house deserves something more than an unsupported statement by the Department of Justice, if it is to be brought forward as justifying this particular legislation.

I say to the house that it would be a tragedy -worse than a tragedy, criminal negligence- if by reason of some technical or constitutional defect students who are anticipating these loans were deprived of the loans. I am not saying that this technicality cannot be overcome. I believe it can be; but I do say if it is not, if doubt is left on this score and as a result some students do not receive loans, it will be a tragedy and an unnecessary deception and arousing of expectations of the young people we are all, I am sure, seeking to aid by this legislation.
The government may well be able to bring forward a convincing argument to offset the opinion I have expressed. I claim no more infallibility than the Department of Justice, or perhaps much less. But I should like to see their answer to my opinion and if it is a convincing one perhaps we can proceed and deal with this legislation as it is. On the other hand, if the government is not assured that the difficulties I have raised are without substance, then I suggest it has a duty to consider seriously the amendment I have suggested and either bring it forward itself, or we will bring forward an amendment and the government can adopt it.
I should like to point out that our objective in bringing up this matter is not to slow down or discredit the legislation. It is exactly the contrary. We have stated that we think there are shortcomings in the legislation, but we are most anxious that the proposals of aid should be as effective as they possibly can be. It is usual, I have no doubt, for the government to look upon suggestions of this sort from members of the opposition with scepticism and a degree of suspicion, but I want to assure them that while, as I say, they may find the answer to the problem, they should give rather serious consideration to it in order that the students of this country shall not be deceived by the defects for which this parliament and this government would be responsible.

speechtext:
The University of British Columbia lies within my constituency of Vancouver Quadra. Last fall 13,600 students registered there for the winter session. This is in addition to any who may have registered during the year for night sessions or summer sessions. This figure represents approximately 10 per cent of the winter enrolments of all Canadian students in this single institution. It is second only to the University of Toronto in the enrolment of English speaking students in Canada. The report of the president, Dr. John B. MacDonald for 1962-63 shows that 9,000 of these students come from homes in the lower Fraser valley and Howe sound sections of the greater Vancouver area. A minimum of 4,600 students therefore come from the outside area and must find accommodation at or near the university. Of course some students from the perimeter of the greater metropolitan area prefer to live on or near the campus, so it is safe to say about 5,000 or more students at the University of British Columbia must find board and room either on the campus or in private homes nearby.
It is anticipated the enrolment in British Columbia beyond grade 12 will more than double during the period of the sixties and will be 37,000 by 1971-72. While Victoria University and the junior colleges of the province will take an increasing number of students, the trend is toward 10,000 students rooming and boarding in the University of British Columbia area in my constituency by the end of the decade. It is for these reasons I want to speak today in this debate.
For the most part, these students come from modest circumstances. Some indeed are poor. They must find every dollar of their university education. Some fall out for a year to earn enough money to continue their education, and some of these never make it back. Some are under great pressure at home to abandon their studies in order to contribute to the meagre earnings of their families. These stories are common on every large campus throughout Canada.
The calendar of the University of British Columbia for the 1963-64 session gives us the basic figures for fees, room and board. From these we can construct the cost of going
[Mr. Brewin.l
to university. The University of British Columbia compares with the level of other major campuses throughout Canada. The university has accommodation on campus for 1,256 male and 750 female students, or approximately 2,000. By doubling up, I think this is increased to about 2,500 students. They occupy quarters ranging from ancient and leaky army huts to fine new brick dormitory buildings with adjacent common rooms and cafeterias. They pay from $472.50 to $630 a session, which is approximately eight months, for board and lodging at the university. Off campus prices for board and room in the neighbouring community are approximately the same, ranging from $65 to $80 per month. Student fees vary with the courses from $346 for arts and science students up to $551 for medical students. In addition, each student pays a $24 alma mater fee and other small club fees. Books and equipment vary with the course and sometimes can be purchased second hand. But a sum of $50 is about rock bottom for books, with applied science and medical students paying two or three times as much each year.
Now, add these all together and we have board and lodging from $472.50 to $630; fees, including the alma mater society from $370 to $575; and books from $50 to $150, with totals ranging from $892.50 to $1,355. Add to this a sum for clothing, medical insurance, sports equipment, transportation and miscellaneous expenses and you will see that the most frugal student in the cheapest course, eating porridge for breakfast and beans for dinner, could hardly get by on $1,200 a session, while $1,800 would cover no more than the essentials for a medical student. To a student earning his or her own way, this means that $1,200 to $1,800 hard cash must be found each year for a minimum of four years. A working student must, therefore, save money at the rate of $300 per month or better in the summer months, often while living away from home, in order to return to university in the fall. In fact, this is an almost impossible assignment. Most students have some assistance from their parents or from bursary, scholarship or loan fund. Were it not for these, they would not be at university.
In 1959, a scholarship plan was introduced in British Columbia by the provincial government. It undertook to pay half the fees of the students with first class honours and one third of the fees of the top 2,000 students with second class honours. The province also

authorized the University of British Columbia to borrow up to $2 million for a student loan fund. Special student funds were also set up to encourage teacher training. The total of provincial assistance was $360,554, exclusive of the university loan fund. It gave assistance to 2,972 students.
On the basis of total student enrolment this represented assistance at the rate of $22.91 per student in British Columbia. On that basis in the same year Newfoundland aided total students at the rate of $109.90. Alberta was next with $107.89 and Quebec with $105.90. Ontario was a poor show at $69.76, but still three times better than British Columbia. We stood in eighth place in that year, 1959. In all the comparative statistics which the Canadian universities foundation presents on this subject, three provinces lead all others by a mile in their efforts to aid students. They are Quebec, Newfoundland and Alberta.
If I may sum up, the province of British Columbia has aided about one quarter of its university students in recent years through scholarships and bursaries, or what are sometimes called money for marks programs. The average assistance per student under these provincial grants is about $126. Spread over the eight months of the university year, this amounts to about 50 cents a day for the bright student who is able to qualify, and that is not enough money to buy a pizza.
While the provinces have been increasing the amount of assistance they have given to students in recent years, it is still small potatoes and few to the hill. British Columbia which I cite because it is my home province, is no better or worse than other provinces. Support for universities and university students is not the favourite cause of provincial politicians. In British Columbia if you stand still they'll pave you; move and they'll award you a construction contract; study and they'll raise your fees.
We should clearly understand that Canadian university students are appealing to us for federal help because their provincial governments are only moderately interested in their welfare. However well the provinces may have met the challenge of educating Canadians through primary and secondary schools, they are a flop by North American standards in providing university education.
As proof of what I say, the Canadian universities foundation has provided me with
Loans to Students
some significant figures. In the state of Washington expenditure on higher education is 1.43 per cent of all personal income. In British Columbia it is 0.20 per cent, or one fifth of 1 per cent. In New York state 1.26 per cent of personal income is spent on higher education while in Ontario the figure is 0.17 per cent, or one seventh as much. Maine spends 1.21 per cent of personal income while New Brunswick spends 0.11 per cent, or one eleventh as much.
In his book, "Higher Education in British Columbia", written in the fall of 1962, President MacDonald of U.B.C. refers to our failure to keep pace in the field of higher education in a different way:
The number of students registered in British Columbia in 1961-62 was 14,710 or 17.7 per cent of the college age population, that is the age group 18-21. This figure compares with 12.3 per cent in Canada as a whole and 39.5 per cent in the United States.
While we in British Columbia may take a small comfort in beating the Canadian average, we as a nation can take no pride at all in the fact that Americans send proportionately three times as many students to colleges and universities. Let it continue and we must become the intellectual inferiors of Americans. We are heading for Lower Slobovia.
Dr. MacDonald goes on to say:
Professional people account for only 6.2 per cent of the Canadian labour force; the proportion in the United States is three times as high, that is 18.6 per cent. In proportion to the size of its population, Canada employs approximately half the number of scientists and engineers employed by the United States.. .Throughout Canada only one half of the matriculants with 70 per cent or better go to university ...Of 100 pupils entering grade II only nine ultimately enter university and onlv 6 graduate.
Dr. MacDonald then compares United States education achievement with Russia, and notes that by the end of the decade they will have twice as many engineers as the United States. If we fall behind the United States and Russia, do we fall behind any other countries? To find this out I obtained some tables of figures from the Canadian universities foundation published by UNESCO, on education at the third level, that is institutions which require completion of a secondary school education for admittance.
These international statistics show Canada in tenth place in the late 1950's in the production of graduates from scientific and technical facilities. Here is a table showing

the number of scientific and technical graduates for the top dozen countries:

United States	96,509
India	70,842

West Germany	15,555

Comparisons in this field are difficult to make and we may argue, perhaps with some validity, that our graduates are better educated, than, let us say, the 6,492 scientific graduates from the Philippines. Let us make another comparison. Norway, Sweden and Belgium are a group of countries comparable to Canada in size and culture and free of the enormous involvement in the nuclear and aerospace industries which distorts comparisons with the United States and Russia.
These little countries have approximately 20 million total population. They enrolled about 82,000 university students compared with 106,000 for Canada in 1960. They had 13,160 students in engineering compared with 15,190 in Canada, and they graduated 4,043 scientific students against 5,609 for Canada. Our standards, then, seem comparable to and perhaps even better than European standards in these respects. But these are qualitative comparisons. We need some qualitative ones if we are to assess our true position.
While we need a steady flow of bachelor graduates from our universities to staff the industrial and highly technical economy in which we live, we must also have a steady flow of master and doctoral graduates, men and women with two or three degrees to teach the oncoming students and to advance our knowledge and technology.
In the United States in 1961-62, there were 420,000 graduated with a first degree, 85,000 graduated with a second or master degree, and 12,000 graduated with a doctorate degree. My figures come from a report by the United States department of health, education and welfare. In Canada in the same year we graduated 23,000 with a first degree, 2,800 with a second degree and only 321 with a third degree, according to Canadian univer-ties foundation figures. On this basis the United States graduates 18 times as many bachelor degrees, 30 times as many master degrees and 38 times as many doctor degrees.

Put another way, the United States is producing senior scholars and scientists at a rate comparable to four times our own.
One measure of the effectiveness of a nation's scientists in fields of peaceful research is the number of Nobel prizes its scientists have won. I have taken the figures from Whitaker's Almanack for 1964 and they do not include the literature and peace awards, but only those for physics, chemistry, physiology and medicine. Since these awards began in 1901 the United States has won 50, Germany 42, The United Kingdom 42, France 16, Netherlands 11, Sweden 8, Russia 7, Austria 7, Switzerland 7, Denmark 5, Italy 4, Hungary 3, China 2, Belgium 2 and Canada 2, who were Dr. Banting and Dr. MacLeod. The latter was dean of medicine at Toronto, under whom Banting worked.
Although he was born and educated in Scotland and returned there, his award is credited to Canada. Ten other nations drew one each of the Nobel awards in science. Thus, were it not for the fortuitous presence in Canada of Dr. MacLeod we would be at the bottom of this most distinguished roster of scientific achievement.
Whatever advantage we may once have held over other nations in the field of education, we are losing it now. We are losing it quantitatively and qualitatively. We no longer produce the numbers of science graduates, doctors and research fellows to remain competitive for very long in the world of modern technology.
United States achievement in higher education has been paid for at the state level at rates far in excess of anything we are prepared to pay at provincial levels in Canada. This means we must inevitably concede intellectual superiority of the Americans if we choose not to pay for education.
Whatever we do here at the federal level to help students through university must be matched by equivalent effort at the provincial level to improve and enlarge their universities. In support of Dr. MacDonald's stirring campaign to awaken our province to the needs and goals of higher education, University of British Columbia students covered the whole province in their "Back Mac" campaign and petitioned the B.C. government with 232,000 signatures. Many people thought "Mac" went too far. He was overdoing his zeal for an educated people.

If I were to dig into the records of other provinces, I would find the same story: overcrowded universities, not enough regional colleges, shortages in faculty and staff, inadequate equipment for teaching and research, underdeveloped postgraduate schools, insufficient funds to support our most brilliant and productive scholars. This student loan program parallels a similar program in the United States called the national defence student loan program. While it is a very general program providing $1,000 a year for five years to any needy student, it has one unique feature. Ten per cent of the value of the loan and accrued interest are cancelled for each year of full time public school teaching service rendered by a student borrower, up to 50 per cent of the value of the loan. The reason of course is to encourage a continuing supply of teachers throughout the nation.
The American preoccupation with universal education of a high level has been a major characteristic of that people throughout their history and the prime factor in their success. Thomas Jefferson said: "By far the most important bill in our whole code is that for the diffusion of knowledge among the people", and he meant it. Benjamin Franklin setting out his rules for success, Lincoln in his log cabin studying by candlelight, Kennedy going down to Harvard to raid the faculty for brain-trusters-all these leaders believed fervently in the power of education to lift the welfare of the people and to increase the power of the nation, and the people in turn believed them and provided for the fullest education of their children. It has made them a great people.
I hope that in this bill we have at last caught a glimpse of that spirit. Samuel Johnson said: "Much can be done with a Scotchman if you get him young enough." I believe this is true of Canadians.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
May I at the
outset say that I am in wholehearted agreement with the purpose this bill is trying to achieve. As I said last Monday when speaking on the federal-provincial fiscal bill for which the Minister of Finance is also responsible, any measure which will contribute to placing the student population of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories on a par with their brothers to the south is welcome indeed.
I may say I am happy to see the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) in his place because I intend to raise one or two points which throw some
Loans to Students
doubt on the applicability of this bill to the student population in the north. In this connection I was much impressed by the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), since his approach in a general sense can be equated with the criticisms I have to offer in a specific sense.
Before I deal specifically with the points I have to make, may I observe that on Monday I spoke at some length with respect to the consultation, or rather the lack of consultation between federal authorities and territorial authorities both in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories, particularly with regard to this type of program. The very next day the minister, when he introduced this measure, said as reported on page 5443 of Hansard:
Accordingly it is our expectation that students seeking loans under the Canada plan will, in each province, file applications through familiar and established channels.
He said, too, that he had invited the help of the provinces, and later that he had ascertained that all the provinces with one exception had come to agreement with him with respect to the provisions of the bill. I wonder what consultation the minister had with education authorities in the Yukon or in the Northwest Territories. I wonder how many explanations were made to those authorities by the government, as they were undoubtedly made to the governments of each of the ten provinces. I wonder if it is the minister's intention to ascertain specifically the views which pertain in those two territories. I notice that the Yukon and the Northwest Territories are lumped together in the calculation which was made when the minister presented this bill. That calculation appears on page 5446 of yesterday's Hansard and shows the amount as being $.08 million. It would be of assistance in my opinion if the minister were to break down this figure so as to show exactly the figure arrived at with respect to each of the territories.
The situation with regard to legislation in the territories is similar to that which arises from the operation of sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. There are constitutional divisions of function between the federal parliament and the legislative assemblies, or councils, if you will, of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. This division of powers is laid down in the Yukon Act, as I am sure the minister knows, and section 16 (r) of that act gives to the legislative council of the territory-a wholly elected council-exclusive jurisdiction to

Loans to Students
legislate with respect to matters pertaining to education in the territory. If we examine the bill before the house it will be seen that its provisions refer to the provinces. Reference is made to the lieutenant governors in council of the individual provinces. Reference is made to specified additional expenditures in the provinces, and the bill refers also to provincial allocations, appropriate authorities in the provinces, and so on.
In my view there is a serious defect in this measure which may prevent its application to the two territories with which I am concerned, particularly to the Yukon. Since the Yukon legislative council has exclusive jurisdiction in matters pertaining to education and since the minister, in the quotation to which I referred in his speech yesterday, calculated an allocation of a portion of the $40 million which will be required for the first year's operation of this plan as far as the Yukon is concerned, it would seem that it is the government's intention that the student loan fund provisions should apply to students in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories as well as in the ten provinces of Canada. I presume that is the intention of the legislation. If the bill is examined in detail it will be seen that reference is made in clause 2(b) to the appropriate authority. It is stipulated that the appropriate authority for a province means-
-such person, body or authority as may be designated by the lieutenant governor in council of that province as the appropriate authority for that province for the purposes of this act.
I realize that the usual argument might be advanced here that a "province" is defined in the Interpretation Act, and therefore it is applicable to the territory. For the purpose of the record I think I might read that definition from the Interpretation Act. Section 35(24) of the Interpretation Act sets forth that-
-"province" includes the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory;
To my mind, however, there is a distinction between "legislature, legislative council or legislative assembly" as defined in section 35(13) of the Interpretation Act, and "executive council", which phrase is used in section 35(15) of the Interpretation Act. The bill places certain delegated authority in the hands of the lieutenant governor of a province. The Yukon has no lieutenant governor, so we go to the Interpretation Act and find

that "lieutenant governor in council" is defined by subsection (15) of section 35 as-
-the lieutenant governor, or person administering the government of the province indicated by the act, for the time being acting by and with the advice of, or by and with the advice and consent of, or in conjunction with the executive council of such province.
I may be wrong when I come to the conclusion that "executive council" means, in effect, the cabinet of a province. The Yukon has no cabinet because it has not developed to that stage of responsible government. So that when we attempt to conclude that the phrase "lieutenant governor in council" as used in Bill No. C-110, the measure before us, is the same thing as saying "the person responsible in the Yukon Territory for the administration and government of the territory", to paraphrase, we find we are unable to do so because of the existence of the phrase "executive council" in section 35(15) of the Interpretation Act. Because it would mean that the minister of northern affairs or his delegate, the commissioner of the Yukon, will have to act by and with the advice of, or by and with the advice and consent of, or in conjunction with the executive council. In fact, the only legislative authority that is passed to the Yukon Territory by the Yukon Act is the power of the elected council exclusively to pass laws with respect to education by the well understood device of the commissioner acting by and with the advice and consent of the legislative council of the territory.
My point here is that by using the phrase "lieutenant governor in council" in this bill, the bill excludes the operation of its provisions with respect to the Yukon Territory. I think this is a serious defect. I think that if the bill is to apply to the Yukon-and particularly the Yukon, because I have studied the situation there, whereas I have not particularly studied that of the Northwest Territories-then it must be clearly spelled out. As I have said, we have no lieutenant governor in council in the Yukon, and I submit we cannot by any stretch of the imagination apply the provisions of the Interpretation Act to cure it.
Another serious defect in the bill results from the fact that there are no institutions of higher learning in the Yukon Territory or in the Northwest Territories. The maximum degree to which education can be taken in the Yukon is up to grade 13. Many of our students on leaving high school with senior matriculation attend the University of Alaska.

Yet I am in some doubt whether the provisions of the measure before us include the University of Alaska, in one of the states of the United States of America. For instance in clause 2(k) "specified educational institution" is defined as meaning-
-an institution of learning, whether within or outside a province-
If those words "outside a province" can extend to mean "outside of Canada", then my point may be groundless. But I have some fears that the intention of the bill does not go that far.
Again in clause 10 of the bill, where it speaks of "a certificate of eligibility", the bill sets forth that-
-the appropriate authority for a province may issue or cause to be issued a certificate of eligibility to a qualifying student for an academic year.
It is my submission that, based on the constitutional defects which I submit exist, it may well be that in this case we arrive at the anomalous situation where the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) must issue or cause to be issued a certificate of eligibility under clause 10 of the bill. Since there is no lieutenant governor in council in the Yukon, and since the provisions of the Interpretation Act do not apply, in my submission, in this instance because of the use of that phrase we must fall back on the minister of the federal government who is responsible for administering the affairs of the Yukon Territory, and I am sure that is not what is intended by the provisions of the bill.
Even if you arrive at that conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that the minister is precluded from acting. Indeed, I would submit the bill would go so far as to preclude his delegate, the commissioner of the Yukon, from acting under the provisions of the bill by the very terms of section 16(r) of the Yukon Act, which resides the exclusive jurisdiction to legislate on matters pertaining to education in the commissioner in council of the Yukon Territory. So whichever way you turn and look at this problem, you come back to the fact that the wholly elected legislative body in the Yukon has exclusive jurisdiction; and yet the use of the phrase "lieutenant governor in council" in the bill before us would purport to expand jurisdiction which does not exist so far as the Yukon is concerned.
When the minister replies to the remarks which have been made I would be grateful if he would clarify the points which I raise here and would reassure me that he has received advice that there is no constitutional
Loans to Students
problem in so far as the applicability of the provisions of this bill are concerned with respect to the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I should like to say that the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) would have been here to speak on the measure himself had he not been called away to visit personally the Pine Point mine. He has now embarked on this rather long journey.
I think a worth-while point to be made here is that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) who immediately preceded me in the debate, mentioned that British Columbia, Quebec and I believe Newfoundland had the most advanced provisions in all of Canada with regard to assisting students through institutions of higher learning. However the minister of northern affairs knows, if the Minister of Finance does not, that in the Northwest Territories there have been in existence for some time provisions whereby a student upon leaving secondary school can obtain a loan of up to $1,500 throughout the term of his or her attendance at university; and, subject only to the provision that such student in receipt of such loan shall return to the Northwest Territories and reside there for four years, the loan becomes an outright grant. It seems that this perhaps would have been a desirable objective in legislation of this kind, although I can just imagine the enormous cost that it would result in. But this legislation in the Northwest Territories is very far reaching indeed because it provides for a workable plan which stimulates an interest in obtaining higher education among the students in the Northwest Territories, and in addition provides an incentive to qualified university graduates to return to the Northwest Territories and assist in creating there a highly educated and permanent population.
One speaks of the drain of brainpower to the United States. Would not some sort of incentive-this, after all, is a federal creation in so far as the Northwest Territories are concerned; certainly the great proportion of the money to support the scheme comes from the federal treasury-if provided in a bill such as this, help to prevent that drain of brainpower? The loan of $1,500 per year for any student in the Northwest Territories wishing to attend university becomes an outright grant if the student, after graduating, returns to the territories and lives there for at least four years. A similar plan has existed for many years in the armed forces.
