With those constitutional arguments and with the request to the minister to reassure me that my fears in this respect are unfounded, I do not intend to pursue the matter further. I would request that he put the points I have made to him to the law officers of his department or to the law officers of the Department of Justice, so they may assess them and assure the educational authorities and the legislative assembly in the Yukon, and the people of the territories generally, that the bill before us applies in the same manner and to the same extent to the territories as it does to the other ten provinces of Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most speakers in this debate have mentioned that they have within their riding a university. I am not in a position to claim that honour, not having any university located in my riding; but I think I can with some accuracy describe my riding as something of a bedroom for the University of British Columbia, in that a great many of the students there do live in my riding, particularly those students who are married, with children, and are going back to school later in life. These people, who are living in my riding in converted basement suites and upstairs rooms, will probably get the greatest benefit from this bill of any class of university student.
Perhaps one of the greatest upheavals, or greatest developments in education in Canada occurred after the second world war with the enactment by a former Liberal government of the veterans charter. Under the veterans charter thousands and thousands of returned veterans who had been deprived of the chance to continue their education by the depression and the oncoming of war were given the opportunity of entering civilian life by going back to school and university. I am sure there are many members in this house today who took advantage of the provisions of the veterans charter. We all know doctors, lawyers, accountants and school teachers who became such because of the veterans charter.
Today we are dealing with a new generation, one which fortunately, I am sure we all believe, has not had to put on the uniform of our country and go to war in defence of Canada; but a generation which nevertheless, in the interests of themselves and in the interests of the nation, needs to have the fullest opportunity of acquiring the best possible education they can get. In Canada we we have long recognized the value of free public education, and in fact required by law
[ Mr. Nielsen.]
that everyone who is capable must be educated to a certain level. It seems to me tragic and illogical that at the very age when continued education and training would be of the greatest benefit, not only to the individual but to the nation, we abandon the concept of free education. Surely it is self-evident to everyone that to leave untrained and unlearned a mind that is capable of training, capable of learning, is the greatest possible waste that we can imagine. And there is waste. Of the over one million people in Canada between 18 and 25 years of age, as the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) pointed out the other day, it is estimated by educational authorities that approximately one fifth are capable of going to university and acquiring or absorbing a university education. However, at the present time approximately only 11 per cent of that group are registered in Canadian universities. Therefore the talents of at least half of our most capable young people are not being fully utilized or developed.
The bill that we have before us today provides, as hon. members know, that in the first year $40 million in loans shall be made available to students in amounts of not more than $1,000. These loans shall be interest free until seven months following graduation, or when the student is no longer a full time student, and are to be repayable on a five to ten year basis.1 This was described by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) the other day as falling far short of what we had said we would do in the last election campaign. This, to me, is only the first step in what we intend to do and want to do in the field of education. It might fall far short at the moment of what we said we would do. I do know however that it goes $40 million beyond what his party did for five years while they formed the government.
This bill is assured, surely, of easy passage through this house. This easy passage has been assisted by the work of the officers of the Canadian union of students who, I think, have become familiar figures around parliament hill during the last few months in talking up the case for university loans. I was happy to make the acquaintance of their former president, David Jenkins and their executive assistant Paul Williamson. All I can say is that the students of Canada are well served by the officers of the Canadian union of students. While I was a student I often mildly objected to the fees we had to pay to what was then the national federation

of Canadian university students, which is now the Canadian union of students. As a member of parliament I now see the value [DOT]of those fees that students pay to their national association.
Because of the easy passage that I think this bill will receive, I do not want to fill the record with a great many figures; but I would like to put one or two on the record, simply to show the need and value of this type of loan program. It has already been said in this debate that the average undergraduate costs per year in Canada run between $1,196 and $1,550, with an average of somewhere around $1,400 per year for a student to go to university. While we in Canada have the phenomenon, which is not common in many other countries, of students working during the summer, the dominion bureau of statistics latest survey shows that the average annual summer savings of students is $507. It is therefore quite obvious that a student has to make up this large gap in order to afford his university education either from a scholarship or loan program, and by assistance from parents or family.
It is obvious to me from these figures that if we are going to provide to all Canadians the opportunity of acquiring a university education, we need this program very badly. If we are going to have equality of opportunity, we cannot leave it any longer simply to students to rely for a substantial part of their income upon their families and parents. If we are going to leave it as it was, many people in Canada are going to be deprived of an education and the opportunity to realize their talents to the full.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) mentioned yesterday-it seems that his speech writer and I read the same material-a survey made by the University of Toronto advisory committee on ex-service students entitled "The Veteran at Varsity", which survey shows that of the normal student population 20 per cent came from the homes of industrial workers, but in the veterans group after the war this figure rose to 32 per cent. In other words the veterans charter program brought about a 12 per cent increase in the number of students from that group of the population whose sons and daughters normally do not attend university. The loan program we are enacting today will have the very same effect as the veterans charter program did in encouraging the sons and daughters of industrial workers to go to university and complete their education.
Loans to Students
People generally often think of the doctor's son and the lawyer's son going to university, but if we are going to realize the talents of Canadians fully, if we are going to have full equality of opportunity we have got to start thinking of the carpenter's son and the plumber's son going to university. I suggest that this program will make this possible, as was demonstrated by the University of Toronto survey with regard to the veterans charter program. That program was implemented by a grateful nation in recognition of the service of those young people who went to war for Canada. I hope that this loan program is simply the first step in the implementation of a civilians charter, as the act of a wise and prudent nation realizing that it is in our own best national interest to see that everyone who is capable of acquiring training and knowledge has the fullest opportunity of doing so.
There is one important aspect of the bill to which I should like to make specific reference. You will note that in the bill there are no residence requirements, except for the fact that the student must be a Canadian citizen or be resident in Canada for one year with the intention of residing in Canada after he ceases to be a full time student.
I am sure there are probably smallminded people who think that there should be some provincial residence requirement and that if, for example, someone is going to borrow money in British Columbia from the provincial allotment of some $3 million he should be a resident of British Columbia. I could not disagree more with this sentiment. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) that in drawing the regulations pursuant to the act he specifically forbid the implementation by provincial authorities of any provincial residential requirement.
I suggest that university education must be looked at nationally and there is no room for narrow provincialism in this field. In this regard a former president of the University of British Columbia, Dr. Norman A. M. Mackenzie, had this to say, and I want to put this quotation on record because I think it is a valuable one:
The work of the universities does not end at the provincial boundaries either in its scope or significance. In each of the larger universities in Canada there are students from all the provinces. In some cases the students from other parts of Canada constitute as much as one third of the total enrolment. Similarly, the graduates of the universities are distributed over the entire country. Anywhere from one fifth to more than one half of the graduates of particular institutions live and work in provinces other than the one in which they received

Loans to Students
their education. University graduates are one of the most mobile elements in the working population and comprise a source of skilled and educated personnel which is available to the nation as a whole. It is well known that the university trained personnel which are needed by governments and by national businesses of all kinds are recruited from every part of the country.
Therefore I repeat to the Minister of Finance that in the regulations under this legislation the provinces must be forbidden from setting up any provincial residence requirement. If we are going to utilize our facilities in Canada, students, as former president Mackenzie said, must be free to move about the country and acquire the best possible education. It is silly to think that in Canada we can build in each province first class institutions of higher learning in every conceivable subject and technique. Students from British Columbia, for example, must be free to go to Montreal for advanced medical training. I would hope there would be students from other parts of Canada who would want to come to British Columbia to study certain specialized fields there.
One of the first acts of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) was to assure the construction of a veterinary college in western Canada to serve the four western provinces. Students from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia must be free to move about and able to apply for loans in order to go to that veterinary college.
I listened with great interest yesterday to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and some of the objections he raised to the bill. I realize that the leader of the New Democratic party is always in a difficult position when the government brings in good legislation. He wants to agree with it but he always has to find something wrong with it. He raised yesterday what I suggest is a red herring in saying that under the provisions of this legislation students would have to go to the banks in order to obtain a loan. This is simply an example of the leader of the New Democratic party desperately searching in an effort to find something wrong with the bill.
As the Minister of Finance pointed out at the time, he felt that the banks would want to establish commercial contact with students and would be anxious to comply with and participate under the provisions of the loan legislation. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam scoffed at this suggestion, but I suggest that the point made by the Minister of Finance was well taken. Surely the interest
[Mr. Basford.l
of the banks in establishing commercial relations with students is demonstrated by the fact that they try very hard to open branches on the university campuses across Canada. I know that at the university I attended they rented space on the campus direct from the university, and they were forever soliciting us to open accounts there in order to establish commercial contact with us.
Surely the interest of the banks is demonstrated by the fact that they advertise very widely in university newspapers and other publications by means of advertisements written in language to appeal to university students so they can get them as customers.
It seems to me there is another point the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam missed in dragging this red herring into the debate on the bill. In the budget speech on March 16 the Minister of Finance made it very clear that the provisions of the proposed student loan legislation would be such as to establish a system under which students would get loans from the banks which would be guaranteed by the government. I should like to repeat what the minister said at that time, as found on page 982 of Hansard:
I believe these loans to university students can be provided most conveniently and efficiently through the chartered banks with their widespread facilities all across the country. We want to enlist the co-operation not only of the banks but through them of the university authorities in order to ensure that all loans are made to full time students capable of proceeding to a degree and in need of financial assistance to carry on their studies. The government is prepared to guarantee these student loans; there are good precedents for such an approach in our other legislation. No interest would be payable by the student during his years of study.
I am sure that the Canadian union of university students, the organization that looks after the interests of Canada's university students, read the budget speech on March 16, are aware of that paragraph and have had notice of the fact for some months that this was the intention of the legislation.
They have not made a complaint. In fact, as all hon. members know, only a few weeks ago a few of us organized a meeting in the building here at which students could present their views to us. They made no objection to the fact that this legislation used the chartered banks as lending institutions. If they have no objection, I think that the objections of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) are really unfounded and, as I suggest, simply a red herring used by a man who wants to find some objection to what is good legislation.

I listened yesterday also with great interest to the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) that this bill is unconstitutional. I simply want to say that I am unimpressed by these arguments. The people of my province want to see provided for their children the best possible educational opportunities, and to do this they are going to need help from the government of Canada and from the parliament of Canada. I personally, and I speak as an individual, am looking to this parliament to provide British Columbians and Canadians generally with the fullest opportunity for graduate and postgraduate schooling.
In order to do this, we must have a strong central government. I am becoming alarmed at the constant attempts we see here to whittle away the power of the central parliament. We are strong Canadians in British Columbia and being Canadians to us means being able to look to Ottawa, to a strong central government, to help us with our problems of education, of welfare and of development. We are not interested in a central government that can only raise taxes and run the post office or contribute to the United Nations. I do not want to see a central government that is solely the tax collector for ten provincial premiers, as seemed to be the suggestion of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam yesterday, when he suggested that this legislation was wrong, that we should have ten provincial scholarship committees. I realize the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has had years of service as a provincial premier and cannot forget this when he gets into the national parliament. If the forces within Canada are such as to succeed in leaving the central government weak and emasculated, then I suggest that an ever increasing number of people in my province are going to begin questioning their relationship with that weak central government.
The adequate provision of undergraduate and postgraduate opportunities in Canada is of national concern, requiring direct national action. The parliament of Canada must have the ability and the willingness to deal with education as a national affair. This bill is a good beginning. But if we are going to develop as a strong nation, we must provide everyone capable of acquiring an education with a maximum amount of facilities and opportunities. In order to provide proper educational opportunities for Canadians, the government of Canada and this parliament
Loans to Students
are going to have to involve themselves directly in the years ahead in providing facilities for that education.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have examined the bill now before us with great care and I question its constitutionality. In my opinion, it is unacceptable, unless major amendments are brought to it.
There are so many ways in which the federal government could help education without having to intrude either directly or indirectly in a matter under provincial jurisdiction.
I feel that the bill, in its present form, is but a sly and underhanded way for the federal government to intrude in the field of education, even if it does provide an option formula for the province of Quebec. As a matter of fact, experience shows that when the federal government enters a field under provincial jurisdiction, things are finished and done with, because it never withdraws.
Instead, I would suggest to the federal government that it should mind its own business and look after it, and that it should try to solve the economic problems now facing the country, especially the low level of income of farmers in eastern Canada and British Columbia and the unemployment we now have.
Mr. Speaker, show me one word, one sentence in the British North America Act which allows Ottawa to intrude into the field of education, either directly or indirectly. Section 93 is abundantly clear, as the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinongd-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) explained perfectly.
Moreover, section 11 in Bill No. C-110 constitutes, in my opinion, a direct intrusion into the field of education, which is exclusively assigned to the provinces. In other words, the federal government is giving instructions to the provinces. In fact, here is what is stipulated in section 11 (1):
The appropriate authority for a province shall not issue or cause to be issued any certificate of eligibility in a loan year-
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether this is not an order given to the provinces, whether it is not a direct intrusion into education, a field under provincial jurisdiction? In other words, the federal government is imposing conditions to the provinces.

Mr. Gerard Filion, of the daily newspaper Le Devoir, wrote on April 18, 1962:
A good point in favour of the Conservative party is its tax sharing policy. The provinces are rightly unsatisfied, but nevertheless, they have gained some ground during the past five years.
And Mr. Filion went on:
Under the logic of events and on the strength of precedents, the Liberal party is slowly but deliberately driving its wedge. A Liberal government in Ottawa would surely increase the intrusion of the central government in the educational field.
Mr. Speaker, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Secretary of State (Mr. La-montagne) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) want by all possible means to take under their control education, which is a provincial responsibility.
According to the Joliette Journal of March 13, 1963, the present Prime Minister stated in Manitoba:
It is necessary to increase assistance to all programs of higher education.
And the newspaper Le Devoir of February 10, 1964 published the following report from Sudbury:
Miss Pauline Jewett, Liberal member for Northumberland, suggested before some 350 teachers of the Ontario federation of high schools, the establishment of a federal department of education.
I would refer hon. members to page 5154 of Hansard, where, with regard to point of privilege I had just raised in the house the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) is shown to have stated:
It is just on that point I would like to disagree. It is a curious thing that in this country with 19 million population we do not have in our federal government a minister of education or a department of education. We have one Minister of Agriculture, with another coming up, but no minister of education. It is not only curious but tragic.
If a man does not get a sound education, let us say in one of the maritime provinces, and becomes unemployable, who is going to be responsible for the maintenance of him and his family?
And the hon. member for York East, who is sitting on the government side, added:
I support this bill very strongly but it seems a devious way, an indirect way to accomplish what we know should be done, and that is for the federal government to be concerned with educational matters. I strongly suggest that all of us, and the government in particular, pay great attention in the contemplated amendments to the British North America Act to work out a scheme by which education will be a national concern and become the business of this government.

At this point, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house listened with attention and interest to the remarks of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto). I am led to believe that he frequently is placed in a position of flying kites for the government, and I am waiting for further support on the other side of the house for this proposition that denies every principle of confederation, that an amendment be made to the British North America Act to provide for the control of education by the federal parliament.
I wonder what is the opinion of the other government members, especially those of the province of Quebec, following the statement made by the hon. member for York East. What is the opinion of the Minister of Justice concerning the eventuality of a federal department of education, as advocated by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett), as well as the hon. member for York East?
We would be very happy to know about it. This bill, unless it is amended so as to make it conformable to provincial jurisdiction in educational matters, seems to me a first step by the government to establish a department of education with a view to taking over provincial responsibilities.
Hon. Donald Fleming, who was minister of finance said on September 6, 1958, as shown on page 4726 of Hansard:
-that this government will always scrupulously respect the terms of the Canadian constitution. It is plainly recognized that education is a field of jurisdiction exclusively assigned to the provinces...
And he went on to say:
As long as this government is in office there will never be any attempt made to trespass on that jurisdiction exclusively vested in the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, some opposition to this bill has been voiced. University students of the province of Quebec, student associations of the province of Quebec have made known their formal rejection of the federal offer of an interest free loan fund for needy students. Those are Quebec universities.
During an interview, Mr. Dave Jenkins, president of the Canadian union of students, stated that the federal government owes $10 million to students in view of its electoral promise, but that this amount could be reimbursed under the form of fiscal deductions allowed to students, students' parents and industries which grant scholarships. According to the president, direct loans to students from the central government are perhaps unconstitutional, because education falls under provincial jurisdiction.

Without infringing upon the provincial jurisdiction in the field of education, the federal government could assist the students by increasing, for instance, the number of positions available within the various departments in Ottawa, so that the students who have summer holidays may earn some money to pay a part of their studies. Those positions could also be distributed in proportion to the number of French speaking students from Quebec, so that they may have their fair share, just like English speaking students.
I am in a position to note the attitude of the Quebec government. We hear no protest from it, and yet, according to he Devoir of February 20, 1964, at the time, Messrs. Le-sage and Gerin-Lajoie were against a federal assistance program for students, because it was an infringement of the provincial field. Why this silence now?
Even on the government side, there is no unanimity; there are conflicting opinions. Is there any need to recall the statement made by the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Pepin), parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
The provinces would be in a better position to carry out this task. However, Ottawa could promote the extension of universities by means of C.M.H.C. loans.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska was speaking according to his conscience and I must commend him for it. I wonder whether the Minister of Justice agrees with the views expressed by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska and whether he does not feel that this bill infringes, directly or indirectly, upon the provincial field?
I know that many members of the house, unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, prefer to submit to party policy. They would rather sacrifice the legitimate yearnings of the provinces to please their party, but they should have the courage to rise against a bill which affects the jurisdiction of the provinces.
That is the kind of co-operative federalism we have at the present time. It is a new form of centralization to hide the interference by the federal government and enable it to progress by infiltration into the fields which belong to the provinces.
May I advise you, Mr. Speaker, to read the book by Mr. Lamontagne on Canadian federalism. As early as 1944, this theorist explained how federalism should operate in Canada.
Loans to Students
In fact, he wrote:
It is therefore the participation of the government in the main functions of the state which must become the general rule (P. 248).
He also wrote this:
The joint participation of all levels of governments in the functions of the state is perfectly consistent with the Canadian constitution (P. 249). The theory of separation of the functions leads either to the splitting up of federalism, by promoting separatism or legislative union, or to the coexistence of isolated governments within the
The joint participation of all levels of government from carrying out properly its responsibilities (P. 246).
That should be told to the voters, because this text is fraught with consequences. I continue:
The doctrine which gives a definition of federalism as being a form of political unification where sovereignty is divided between several governments having their own exclusive fields of jurisdiction is therefore unacceptable. That definition might satisfy the minds looking above all for clearcut formulas. It may have tallied with a factual situation in the past, but it can no longer fit the present realities. (P. 246)
And he added:
Separation of government functions laid down as a general principle is inconsistent with the social and economic situation or with an efficient political regime.
That is what we have at the present time. I understand that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) engineered the scheme, that he acted as a go-between, sent to the government of Quebec to have them accept this biU.
I wonder if it is true that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) has been the genius who forced the province of Quebec to accept this bill.
Mr. Speaker, it will be noted that since coming into power, the Pearson government has given a perfect illustration of its thinking on co-operative federalism. It does not violate the constitution unilaterally; it proposes to the provinces to assist them in fulfilling their obligations (loans to municipalities, interest free loans to students) or it solicits their acceptance of a bill in a field of concurrent jurisdiction (pension fund).
But everyone knows what happens gradually to co-operation between unequal partners. The central government already has such powers and revenues that co-operation will shortly develop into an implicit centralization system: Ottawa will initiate, legislate and establish new institutions; the provinces will be entrusted with the execution and the distribution of funds.

Loans to Students
Twenty years, ten years of co-operative federalism and the provinces will, in fact, only be administrative and managing agencies.
That is why I contend that co-operative federalism is but another disguised formula for centralization, where the provinces would only be Ottawa subsidiaries whose functions would only be to apply the decisions made in Ottawa.
However, as a result of the federal-provincial conference which took place between the Canadian provinces and the central government, there was agreement on this particular point, namely that the matter of education came under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, that it was the most urgent problem and that it should have priority in our present economic situation. It is recognized that the provinces have the priority in that field and must have the taxation powers they need to meet their obligations.
I wonder why the Quebec government has remained silent about that bill and I find its attitude very surprising.
Last night 1 listened to the speech made by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien). As reported on page 5482 of Hansard, he said:
-the Minister of Finance prepared a bill in accordance with the two following principles which are of the utmost importance:
(a) education comes under the provinces while credit is a matter of federal jurisdiction;
And yet credit is a field of joint jurisdiction, it comes under both the federal and provincial governments. If the hon. member wanted to talk about the provinces' taxation sources when he mentioned credit, he will admit that the provinces have the priority in the field of taxation.
The province of Quebec is well organized today as far as scholarships are concerned. The St. Jean Baptiste society has more than $1.5 million in funds and through the students' honour loan has organized subscription drives to enable students to get scholarships. Loans are made also by the Artisans society and the province of Quebec itself has an excellent system of scholarships. The banks, the credit unions as well as the private sector make loans to students. There is also the provincial arts council. In short, there are in Quebec more than 50 organizations which make loans to students to enable them to continue their studies.

I am afraid that by infringing too much upon that field which does not come under its jurisdiction, the federal government will be the cause of certain abuses.
Mr. Speaker, if the government and the Minister of Finance were so anxious to assist education they could have done it much more simply. They did not have to introduce such a complicated bill which will require the establishment of a group of civil servants whose function it will be to inspect the provinces' bookkeeping in order to ensure compliance with the federal statute.
Since all the provinces have established a system of scholarships within their jurisdiction, the minister could have said for instance: "Starting tomorrow, the central government will pay directly to the provincial treasury the interest on loans granted by each province."
The provinces have the necessary funds to grant loans and the federal government could have assumed the interest costs by reimbursing the provincial ministers of finance for such expenses. Had he done so, there would have been no violation of provincial jurisdiction and the provinces would have been satisfied. Everybody would have been happy, including the students.
I am not surprised to see that Mr. Lesage neither protests nor says anything about this. In fact, an editorial which came to my attention reads as follows:
The reason is that Mr. Jean Lesage is the originator of that scheme which was adopted by the Liberal party in 1958. Mr. Lesage has the dubious honour of having been the first Liberal to advocate the main plank of the platform which carried Mr. Lester B. Pearson to office.
"Free education at all levels".
Mr. Lesage was at that time federal member for Montmagny-L'Islet; he had been previously Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Mr. Lesage was the first person to ask the Liberal party, at this convention, to introduce a bill enabling the federal government to find its way into the education field, which belongs exclusively to the provinces.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to pay a tribute to the Barrette government who, during the short time they were in power, adopted seven or eight important pieces of legislation to assist and stimulate education in the province of Quebec.
I do not agree with certain members who pass judgment on everything that was done in the educational field in the province of Quebec, before 1960.

Indeed, the province of Quebec has weak spots like all other provinces. Under its educational system before 1960 the province of Quebec has provided the church and the state with valuable men, men who have been sitting here as members of the federal government.
I do not think it logical for certain members to criticize what has been done in the educational field in the province of Quebec and to show such confidence in the new system. The new educational system in Quebec will certainly have some flaws; at the present time, the taxpayers are already complaining loudly.
May I be allowed, in concluding, to point out the financial needs of education in the province of Quebec.
Education has priority for all Canada, and Quebec is no exception. From now until 1967 we will have to find $500 million if we want to remain in the world competition for education, the goal being set for the year 1970.
I have a report here on a study prepared by the planning office of the department of education entitled: "Financial Needs of Education in Quebec, 1964-67". It comprises 81 pages of text where, through vital statistics and financial projections, an attempt is made to establish, first of all, the probable cost of education during the next three years, and to study the means that could be used to meet those costs or to reduce them.
Let me quote a few passages of this brief which is very revealing:
Overwhelming forecasts. This study contains Important findings to the effect that:
1.	From the year 1956-57 to the year 1966-67, the total cost of education in the province will increase fourfold, from $286 million to $1,203 million.
2.	In 1966-67, if education had to be satisfied with present sources of revenue and at present rates, there would be a shortage of $245 million to meet the expenditures anticipated.
This applies only to the province of Quebec.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, it is so important for the federal government to make sacrifices and return to the provinces part of their taxing power. That would not mean that we would forget the poorer provinces, and I am sure that the rich provinces of Canada would agree that the federal government should give a certain amount to the other provinces, in order to make up for their financial deficiency.
Again, I quote:
3.	Those increases are due not only to the inevitable increase in the number of students, but also to the increase of the average cost per student. On the other hand, this rise is due to two main factors:
Loans to Students
(a)	More and more students take courses which are costly to establish-we will deal with this matter in a moment-
(b)	For the same program, the unit costs are increasing and will continue to increase because salaries are improving-
Other facts are also worth mentioning. It states, for instance, that school boards will show deficits of $66 million this year. It also points out that, as far as school boards are concerned, the average cost per student increased last year, compared to the previous year, by $38 and that three quarters of that increase, or $27, are due to salary increases granted to the teaching staff. Finally, it states that the average cost per student will amount, this year, to $362 in educational institutions, to $461 in private institutions, to $1,031 in technical and trade schools and to $1,839 in universities.
Finally, it should be mentioned that the financial conditions revealed by this departmental survey are not favourable, since they are making our school system lag and, in many places, necessary solutions are more difficult to apply; let us remember the conclusion arrived at by the organization for economic co-operation and development: A real revolution in education is shaping up in the world under the combined pressure of economic expansion and the yearning for knowledge. It will reach its climax in 1970, when the whole world will be getting an education.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there are statistics concerning the rising cost of education in Quebec and the increasing number of students, but I will not impose on the house by reading them into the record.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, the people of Quebec are concerned when they see the federal government trying more and more to enter and control every field, even where it has no jurisdiction, because when the federal government sets foot in a field, it never gets out but stays there. We are therefore afraid, in the province of Quebec, that this intrusion in the educational field, which, anyhow, did not start today, will result in the creation of a federal department of education.
In some provinces, the French minorities have been fighting for years to obtain recognition of their school rights. That is why, Mr. Speaker, we do not want the majority of this country, which has neither our culture nor our language, to impose its views upon us in the educational field.
The people of the province of Quebec, therefore, want the directives in the educational field to come from the French speaking majority, and not from the English speaking majority. That is the problem. And that is why we have confederation. The province of Quebec has a very different concept of those issues.
There would be a way to correct the situation, but the government makes it more complicated, embittered and creates separatism in the province of Quebec, particularly

Loans to Students
by having no regard lor its rights. If the other provinces are ready to give up their rights, it is up to them. But the people of Quebec are justified in opposing that.
If we want to have a strong confederation and stop separatism, let us return to the provinces, and particularly Quebec, their taxation powers, so that they can develop according to their mentality and conscience.
Mr. Speaker, this government through its constant encroachments on fields that are none of its business, is one of the main causes of the separatist wave that we have in Canada.
As I said earlier, if it is in the interest of English provinces to understand that, it is also in the interest of the federal government to understand that question. If Quebec is strong, Canada will also be strong. And if Quebec is strong, it will hold out better against the American domination. In Quebec we do not want American domination. In English provinces, 80 per cent of television programs originate from the United States and invade Canadian homes. It is impossible for us to accept that. Of course, it is possible, but we prefer to listen to C.B.C. programs, because they are broadcast in our own language.

Mr. Speaker, it is easy for me to answer this question. Not only the province of Quebec, but all the other Canadian provinces suffer from foreign control, since practically 65 per cent of all investments in Canada come from outside. From the standpoint of the economy we are unfortunately an American subsidiary at the present time, and the danger is there.
I wonder what the Minister of Finance does to encourage and help Canadians to regain control of their economy. Our natural resources are developed by foreigners. I am not against foreign capital but foreigners should understand that there should be Canadians on the board of directors.
I would not want the Cuban experience and that of other South American countries to be repeated here in Canada.
With regard to the bill, Mr. Speaker, I am personally against it, in its present form, and I urge the Minister of Finance to amend it and fill in the gaps.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere and other members proved to the house that this bill constitutes an intrusion into an exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
If the government refuses to accept the amendments which will be moved, or does not itself amend the bill, I will not be able to support it, because Quebeckers, and especially the population of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, share my opinion.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-110 is intended to help students of slender means. I admit that the purpose of the

bill is most commendable, but I think that the ways are much less so. If it had not been for those special circumstances, this bill would even be a step toward an improvement in the condition most students had to face for so long.
Those who come from modest families, who succeeded in completing their studies and were able to cross the barrier of segregation at school, know how difficult it was for a lonely young man to reach the institute of technology, the university and even to complete high school. If we remember those sad years, it was the era of castes, of boys with wealthy fathers and of upstarts. It was either money, or academic and political pull which determined the degree of intelligence of the young student. I can tell you that several of the stars of that time would cut a sorry figure if they had to pass the intelligence tests used today. Progress is putting things right. We are confident that thanks to all the changes in education in general and all the facts known to future students, the next generation will find more justice.
Far from me to think that everything will be perfect. But the sole fact that we make efforts to reach perfection, gives hope to our young people. Therefore, it is our duty to remain careful at all times in order not to give up our birthright for a mess of potage, as an excuse to help students. Hence, it is important for us people from Quebec to make sure that our provincial rights in the field of education are not gobbled up once more by the federal ogre.
That is why we, the members of the Rallie-ment Creditiste, objected to the bill under study. At that time we had already discovered another intrusion, hidden as usual. We have always been pioneers in the protection and reconquest of the rights of the province of Quebec and we shall carry on the good work.
In Le Devoir of July 15, which for once, does justice to us, one can read on the editorial page, the following article by Mr. Paul Sauriol:
It is almost unanimously that the House of Commons passed Monday, on first reading, the bill establishing loans for students. If the resolution was passed on division, it was at the request of the Ralliement Creditistes which objects to this new federal intrusion into the provincial jurisdiction. Three of the four groups in the opposition joined the Liberals to approve this measure. This vote throws some light on some recent speeches on co-operative federalism.
Mr. Speaker, the bill states clearly that the provinces remain free to set up their own students' loan scheme. Such a scheme
Loans to Students
has been in operation for a few years already in our own province. However, the possibilities in Quebec are too limited, precisely on account of the action of the federal government in Quebec.
I hope that bill will be one more opportunity for the federal government to make up for its unfairness in the field of education by giving back to Quebec its share of taxes collected in our province.
The best would be for the present government to give back to each province which so desires its taxation right. But as long as we have those two old finance parties, which have never been honest enough to give back what they borrowed, we will remain in the sad obligation of accepting the crumbs which will fall from the table of the champions of centralization.
We realize that such socialist penetrations please certain provinces and that explains why this government, in spite of their fine electoral promises, infringe more and more upon exclusive provincial fields.
Our greatest concern at this time is to know when that widening of powers will come to an end. Why, even at the last election the Liberals presented themselves as the champions of the return of taxation rights to provinces. It was the end of the famous joint plans.
What happened since? In all provincial exclusive fields, we have seen a succession of casual encroachments upon the jurisdiction of Quebec. The Ralliement Creditiste made every effort to delay, if not to check that take-over of the various strongholds of the province of Quebec, but the federal Liberals, implicitly supported by Quebec Liberals, have continued their advance under the camouflage of co-operative federalism, which should rightly be called compressive federalism.
Luring the people with alleged benefits they took advantage of the situation to crawl into the very foundation of our provincial structure.
Even today it is clear that our students, like our school boards, our municipalities and even our province itself need the assistance expected from their government. But do you really help people when you sentence them to bear the yoke of banks for the rest of their lives?
Yet that is what we are doing when we give chartered banks permission to finance the education of our young people. And we

Loans to Students
even go further, since this government guarantees to the chartered banks that they will be the only institutions to enjoy such a privilege.
Mr. Speaker, do you not think it would be much more logical to order the Bank of Canada to put the necessary funds at the disposal of the provinces, so as to allow them to act according to the aspirations and the thinking of their respective population? Several hon. members have asserted that the provincial rights were protected. But in order to pay interest on these loans, we all know very well that the federal government will again levy the necessary taxes in these same provinces.
It is therefore another door open to the federal government in the taxation fields reserved to the provinces.
It is precisely at that level that we are fighting against that interference tolerated by our provincial governments, not to say approved by them and the members who are supporting that bill now.
It is precisely at that stage that we can protect the fortress; it is not only a matter of preventing it from being overrun but also of preventing even arrows from hitting it. By what right, I ask you, does the federal government take it upon itself to tax the people of Quebec, giving them back too often only the third of what it collects from them and offering them small compensations such as free assistance which it considers a fabulous gift?
With Bill No. C-110, as with all other legislation concerning joint programs, it is false to say that the rights of the province of Quebec are protected by the contracting out formula, because the basic encroachment upon the field of taxation bears evidence to the fact that the federal government will again be in control and take the final decisions in this matter.
I should like to quote another extract of Mr. Paul Sauriol's article which was published in Le Devoir:
-a provision under which the federal government will compensate any province which administers its own scheme of student loans.
That is what is called respect for the provincial rights. Such a system remains unacceptable because the central government acts on its own in fields which come exclusively under the provincial jurisdiction, collecting and using taxes for provincial purposes, subjecting to its control and to its schemes even the provinces which would wish to break loose from them.
Let us, once and for all, return the rights to the provinces where they belong and the
[Mr. Gauthier.l
war of rights will come to an end. Thus, the federal government will stop being a mock Santa Claus.
We are longing for the day when the Quebec government will stop playing the game of totalitarian federalism, when we shall at last have in Quebec a government with sufficient courage to get rid of those old tax-mongers.
If each government would keep to its own field, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in either field everything would be in order.
We firmly object also, throughout the province, to these being subjected to the will of bank managers. In order to get out of an abyss, we will be walking near the edge of a more dangerous precipice.
Let us imagine a student coming from a family in receipt of public welfare payments. What impression will he make on the bank manager when he answers the long list of questions asked by the chartered banks in the course of their investigations? If the father does not have a bank account or does not have his bank account in such and such a bank or, which is worse, if he never had a bank account, what will happen?
In these circumstances the degree of intelligence would be determined tomorrow by the chartered banks trust which would control in this way the whole direction of our future thinking.
After giving to chartered banks the power to create all our credit, the control of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation over our small home owners, the control of the Farm Credit Corporation over our agriculture, the control of our industrial life and and even the control of our vital index, today you ask them to control the training of our young people.
You dramatize.
We are realists.
A youth anxious to make his dreams come true will be tied to the worst trust which now controls us completely, and tomorrow will even control our thinking.
This is a nice speech, but I should like to know who wrote it.

It is certainly not a demagogue like the hon. member for Lotbiniere, for he always repeats the same nonsense and always practices the same demagogy. Why does he not try to become more responsible?
Therefore, we take exception, Mr. Speaker, not to the necessary assistance provided for students, but to the hypocritical manner in which the bill was introduced. Why is it that

when Quebec needs something to survive, it has to come and get it from the central government which decides the quantity and quality?
The idea is repugnant to us. And that is why we denounce this federalist oppression.
In conclusion, I ask the minister to authorize the Bank of Canada to make available to the provinces the necessary amounts for educational grants, and I repeat, for educational grants. Students should not be given loans but grants, because a loan is not assistance, it is a trap.
The government should respect the terms of confederation and return taxation rights to Quebec and everybody will be happy. [Text]
